subject: Climate & Environment
title: Countries Leading the Transition
description: A quick win: understand Countries Leading the Transition.

hook.text: Iceland runs almost entirely on renewable energy. Geothermal and hydro do the heavy lifting.

buildup.text: Costa Rica has generated over 98% of its electricity from renewables for years.

discovery.text: Denmark exports surplus wind power to neighbors and aims for 100% renewables by 2030.

twist.text: China installs more solar each year than the rest of the world combined.

climax.text: No single model works everywhere — geography, wealth, and politics shape each path.

punchline.text: The leaders prove it's possible. The rest just need a push.

quiz.question: Which country has generated over 98% of electricity from renewables for years?

details.summary: Countries like Denmark, Iceland, Norway, Uruguay, and Costa Rica generate nearly all their electricity from renewables. China leads in total installed capacity, and India is the fastest-growing major market. Each nation's path reflects unique geography, policy, and economic conditions.
details.whyItMatters: Global examples demonstrate that high renewable shares are achievable in diverse settings. Studying leaders helps other countries design effective energy transition policies.
takeaways: Several countries already run on nearly 100 percent renewables
China has the world's largest installed renewable capacity
Policy support and geography drive national transition speeds

faq.question: How does Denmark generate so much wind power?
faq.answer: Denmark invested early in wind energy with strong government policy, community ownership models, and strategic North Sea placement. Wind now supplies over 50 percent of its electricity. Grid interconnections with Norway and Sweden handle intermittency.

faq.question: Can large industrial countries achieve 100 percent renewables?
faq.answer: Studies show it is technically feasible for countries like the US, Germany, and China with a combination of solar, wind, storage, and grid upgrades. The main barriers are political will, incumbent industry resistance, and the pace of infrastructure build-out.
